nameStory: Staurodesmus dickiei doesn't have a widely-used common name, as it's a microscopic algae that most people never see without special equipment. The scientific name honors Scottish botanist George Dickie, who made important contributions to algae research in the 1800s. Like many microscopic organisms, it's known primarily by its Latin name in the scientific community.
description: Staurodesmus dickiei is a single-celled green algae so tiny you'd need a microscope to see it clearly. This microscopic organism lives in freshwater and has a distinctive star-like or cross-shaped appearance when viewed from above. Each cell is typically divided into two symmetrical halves connected at the center, with small projections or spines extending outward. You won't spot individual cells with the naked eye, but large populations might create a slight greenish tint in very still water.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are invisible to the naked eye, requiring magnification of at least 100x to observe clearly

idTips.label: Star-shaped form
idTips.description: Under magnification, cells appear roughly star-shaped or cross-like with symmetrical projections

idTips.label: Two-part structure
idTips.description: Each cell consists of two mirror-image halves joined at a narrow center point

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Individual cells appear bright green under the microscope due to chlorophyll

idTips.label: Still water habitat
idTips.description: Found floating in very calm, nutrient-poor freshwater with little to no current

habitat: This microscopic algae lives in clean, still freshwater environments like quiet ponds, bog pools, and the calm edges of lakes throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-poor waters with low pollution levels, often in more remote or undisturbed areas. You're most likely to find it in the shallow, sun-warmed waters of small woodland ponds or in the quiet backwaters of larger bodies of water.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase. Best time to collect samples as cells are actively reproducing.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are most favorable for growth and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into early fall but begin declining as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent from the water column, surviving as resistant spores in bottom sediments until spring.

funFact: Despite being a single cell smaller than the width of a human hair, Staurodesmus dickiei can reproduce by literally splitting itself perfectly in half, with each half regenerating the missing pieces to create two identical organisms - nature's most precise photocopying!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it can be confused with other desmid algae, but Staurodesmus species have their distinctive star-like projections while similar Cosmarium species are more rounded. Remember: if it looks like a tiny green star or cross, think Staurodesmus.
contextualKnowledge: This organism belongs to a group called desmids, which are considered living jewels of the freshwater world due to their intricate, geometric beauty when viewed under magnification. Many pond water samples that appear clear to the naked eye are actually teeming with these microscopic architectural marvels.
compareHints: Staurodesmus dickiei is distinguished from its relatives by its specific spine arrangement and overall cell proportions. Unlike S. triangularis which has a more triangular outline, or S. cuspidatus with longer, more pointed projections, S. dickiei has a more balanced star-like appearance. The exact spine length and cell dimensions require careful microscopic measurement to distinguish definitively from closely related species.
